combien que le premier qui en a parlé, à sçavoir Marianus, ayt esté Escossois, c'est à dire Irlandois comme nous parlons aujourd'huy, & que son sentiment ait esté receu en toutes naons indifferemment : quand il dit, que le Roy d'Espagne Recared embrassant le Christianisme envoya sa Couronne au Pape Felix: sans considerer que Recared estoit né dans la profession du Christianisme, & qu'il ny a point eu en son temps de Pape nommé Felix; quand il feint, que par le livre des Actes il appert, que les peuples se [?]ettoient aux pieds des Apostres, & que S. Chrysostome tient que S. Pierre a refusé de Corneille l'honneur qui luy estoit deu, &c.
units.tr: But far from having deigned to take things in this way, they have made a point of verifying that if favour has little value, hatred and anger have none at all. The author of the popular error, published under the name of Sieur de Remond, carried away by the storm of this bad passion, has done what he could to make himself unworthy of all belief. 1. By supposing things entirely false: as when he maintains that for three, even four hundred years no one spoke of the Papess, although Marianus was not two hundred years removed from the time when she is thought to have lived; when he translates Schedel, a formal enemy of the Hussites, as though he were imbued with their sentiments; when he accuses Clauser (for whose good faith the Greek edition of Chalcondyles speaks) of having inserted of his own into the Latin version the account of the Papess; when he assures us that Musaeus cites the Sibyls; when he wants English to pass for Constantine[?] the Great, who died 124 years before the first irruption of the English into Great Britain; when he denies that Otto of Freising, who makes express mention of the Papess in chapter 35 of book 7, wrote anything about it; when he attributes to the Emperor Valens a lieutenant named Bartes; when he wants Anastasius the Librarian to be that priest and cardinal who was condemned in the year 853 by Pope Leo IV, and afterwards opposed Benedict III; when he describes the French as Vincent of Lérins, who died before the French had come into Gaul as far as the Seine; when he writes that the little book of Benno, imitated by Sigebert, who died on 5 October 1113, was forged in Luther's time; when (directly contrary to the testimony of the Ecclesiastical Historians) he attributes to the Council of Nicaea that it made and confirmed the laws of celibacy; when he charges the Germans (whom he depicts as excessively given to debauchery) with alone having made mention of the Papess, although the first who spoke of her, namely Marianus, was a Scot, that is to say an Irishman as we speak today, and his view was received indifferently in all nations; when he says that the King of Spain Reccared, embracing Christianity, sent his crown to Pope Felix, without considering that Reccared was born in the profession of Christianity, and that there was no Pope named Felix in his time; when he feigns that by the Book of Acts it appears that the people threw themselves at the feet of the Apostles, and that St Chrysostom holds that St Peter refused the honour that was due to him from Cornelius, etc.

units.la: 2. En descouvrant qu'il n'avoit jamais eu un vray goust ni des auteurs, ni des histoires qu'il a ou pretendu citer, ou citées. Comme quand il nomme Rabanus Maurus, Iean Rabanus,& le fait disciple de Beda, à la mort duquel il n'estoit pas nay : quand confondant Theophanes auteur Grec avec nostre Freculfe de Lifieux, il l'appelle Theophanus Freculfus, & transforme Paschasius Ratbertus en Passeratius ; Gildas en Gildus ; Burchard de Dorcefter en Burgard ; Neotus Edulphus en Nectus ; Asserius Meneviensis, en Asserinus Manebensis ; Thierry de Metz contemporain d'Otton I en Theodoricus Nicus ; Valram de Naumbourg, en Vltramnus Norimbergensis ; Nicetas adversaire de Leon IX en Nicolas ; Iean de Sarisbery Evefque de Chartres, en Ioannes Saborensis : Honoré d'Auftun , eHannonius Augustodiniensis ; Hildebert E vesque du Mans , en un Hidelberg ; Geli mer Roy des Vandales,en Galinerius; Rab bi David Kimhi , en Kimbius; Moschus eMoseus ; Sunamith nom d'une citadine de Sunem , en Simonite nom propre de fem me; Aradus Isle, en une ville mal nommée
units.tr: 2. By revealing that he never had a true taste either for the authors or for the histories that he has either claimed or cited. As when he names Rabanus Maurus John Rabanus, and makes him a disciple of Bede, at whose death he was not yet born; when, confusing Theophanes, a Greek author, with our Freculf of Lisieux, he calls him Theophanus Freculfus, and turns Paschasius Radbertus into Passeratius; Gildas into Gildus; Burchard of Worcester into Burgard; Nothelm, Edulf, into Nectus; Asser of Menevia into Asserinus Manebensis; Theodoric of Metz, a contemporary of Otto I, into Theodoricus Nicus; Walram of Naumburg into Vltramnus Norimbergensis; Nicetas, an adversary of Leo IX, into Nicolas; John of Salisbury, Bishop of Chartres, into Ioannes Saborensis; Honorius of Autun into Hannonius Augustodiniensis; Hildebert, Bishop of Le Mans, into Hidelberg; Gelimer, King of the Vandals, into Galinerius; Rabbi David Kimhi into Kimbius; Moschus as Moseus; the Shunammite, the name of a woman of Shunem, into Simonite, a proper name for a woman; Arados, an island, into a city wrongly named.

units.la: Item quand il fonde sa pretendue preuve sur des pieces , ou perduës,comme la le- gende de S. Martial escritte par Aurelian ; ou Apocryphes , comme les Epistres attribuées au mesme S. Martial,& arguées de faux par les Cardinaux Baronius, Bellarmin,&c. le pretendu Concile de Rome sous S. Silvestre; les Recognitions de Clement condamnées par S. Athanase en sa Synopse, & par le Concile de Rome sous le Pape Gelase , qui les rejette sous le nom d'Itineraire de S. Pierre, & par le Cardinal Humbert contre Nicetas , & par tous les Doctes modernes : Les escrits du pretendu Abdias Babylonien , releguez entre les livres defendus par le Pape Paul IV l'an 1559.
units.tr: Likewise, when he founds his alleged proof on documents that are either lost, such as the legend of St Martial written by Aurelian, or apocryphal, such as the Epistles attributed to the same St Martial, which the Cardinals Baronius, Bellarmine, etc. have argued to be forgeries; the alleged Council of Rome under St Silvester; the Recognitions of Clement, condemned by St Athanasius in his Synopsis, by the Council of Rome under Pope Gelasius, which rejects them under the name Itinerary of St Peter, by Cardinal Humbert against Nicetas, and by all the learned moderns; and the writings of the alleged Abdias of Babylon, relegated among the forbidden books by Pope Paul IV in the year 1559.

units.la: 3. Quand il attribue au Pape Innocent I, les paroles escrites 74 ans apres sa mort , par le Pape Gelase premier à l'Empereur Anastase , & celles qu'Innocent III a (l'an 1205, 1205, qui estoit le 686 apres le decez d'In-nocent I) inserées en sa lettre à l'Empereur Baudouin I.
units.tr: 3. When he attributes to Pope Innocent I the words written seventy-four years after his death by Pope Gelasius I to the Emperor Anastasius, and those which Innocent III inserted in his letter to the Emperor Baldwin I in the year 1205, 1205, which was the 686th year after the death of Innocent I.

units.la: 4. Quand il fait de nostre Severus Sulpitius, moine habitué à Primuliacum, entre Touloufe & Eauze, un Archevesque de Bourges; & s'imagine que Bergomas vivoit apres l'an 1500: que le Dante (nay seulement l'an 1260) escrivoit l'an 1250, que Nicephore (posterieur de 150 ans à S Bernard) vivoit devant luy: que Pomponius Lætus contemporain de Sabellicus, estoit un ancien auteur comme Tacite, Seneque, Suetone, Lampridius, Spartian, & Eutrope avec lesquels il l'accouple; que l'auteur du livre intitulé des Ceremonies sacrées, à sçavoir Christophorus Marcellus electus Corcyrensis, c'est à dire, eleuà l'Archevesché de Corfou, s'appelloit M. Electus, &c.
units.tr: 4. When he makes our Severus Sulpitius, a monk living at Primuliacum between Toulouse and Eauze, into an Archbishop of Bourges; and imagines that Bergomas lived after the year 1500; that Dante (born only in 1260) wrote in the year 1250; that Nicephorus (150 years later than St Bernard) lived before him; that Pomponius Laetus, a contemporary of Sabellicus, was an ancient author like Tacitus, Seneca, Suetonius, Lampridius, Spartianus and Eutropius, with whom he couples him; that the author of the book entitled Sacred Ceremonies, namely Christophorus Marcellus electus Corcyrensis, that is, elected Archbishop of Corfu, was called M. Electus, etc.

units.la: 5. Quand (pour impugner le Roman de Marianus) il oppose le silence de Rabanus, Strabo, Haimo, Freculphus, Paschasius, &c. ignorant que Rabanus est mort le 4 Fevrier 856, Strabo l'an 849, Haimo le 28 Mars 853, Paschasius le 26 Auril 851; & qu'Heirard successeur de Freculphe en l'Evesché de Lifieux souscrivoit au Concile de Soissons le 26 Auril 853. tout cela devant le temps que Marianus affigne à sa Ieanne, ou arrivé ou expiré; de façon que quand elle auroit esté, ces auteurs n'auroient peu parler ni pour ni contre elle.
units.tr: 5. When, to impugn the romance of Marianus, he opposes the silence of Rabanus, Strabo, Haimo, Freculphus, Paschasius, etc., not knowing that Rabanus died on 4 February 856, Strabo in 849, Haimo on 28 March 853, and Paschasius on 26 April 851; and that Heirard, successor of Freculphus in the bishopric of Lisieux, subscribed to the Council of Soissons on 26 April 853. All this happened before the time which Marianus assigns to his Joan, whether her arrival or her departure. So that even if she had existed, these authors could not have spoken either for or against her.

units.la: Qui d'entre tous ceux qui ont fait quelque estat de Marianus, auroit peu renoncer à son sentiment, voyant la supposition qu'il a faite de sa Ieanne attaquée par un adversaire si mal afforti, que sa langue seule se trouve plus longue que tout son corps, & son escrit si miserable, que qui en auroit retranché les injures & les beveües, l'auroit reduit en un vray squelete? Mais si la procedure virulente de cet homme injurieux, & de tous ceux qui (à son imitation) ont fait ou pourroient faire parade de leur fougue, ou de leur bave; à desgoufté les esprits ennemis des tumultes, & de la tyrannie des passions humaines; la verité prenant la parole pour soy mesme ne leur pourra jamais desplaire, sur tout estant proposée par ceux qui ont esté (comme anterieurs à toutes les fictions sur lesquelles on s'est fondé depuis, & entierement sans interest) plus capables de luy rendre tesmoignage; & sur leur rapport je m'asseure que personne ne sera difficulté de tenir pour fable, ce qui l'est en effet.
units.tr: Who among all those who have held Marianus in any esteem could have given up his opinion, seeing the supposition he made of his Joan, attacked by an adversary so ill-matched that his tongue alone is longer than his whole body, and his writing so wretched that, if one cut away its insults and blunders, it would be reduced to a true skeleton? But if the virulent conduct of this insulting man, and of all those who (in his imitation) have made or could make a show of their fury or their foam, has disgusted minds hostile to tumults and to the tyranny of human passions, then truth, taking up the word for itself, will never displease them. This is especially so when it is set forth by those who were (being earlier than all the fictions on which men have since relied, and wholly disinterested) most capable of bearing witness to it. And on their report I am confident that no one will have difficulty in holding as fable what really is fable.

units.la: Reste que nous taschions (s'il se peut) de descouvrir la porte par laquelle elle s'est introduite dans la creance des hommes. L'Histoire d'Erford {1}parlant de Iean VIII successeur d'Adrian II, tient ce langage, Sous le mesme Roy Charles le Gros, le Pape Iean celebra un Concile à Erford, Hildebert (ou plustost {2}Luitbert) estant Archevesque de Mayence l'an 880. Notez: ce Pape a esté femme, & seroit le VIII, s'il estoit compté entre les autres. Et le Cardinal Baronius portant sa visée sur le mesme objet, joint sa remarque en ces termes {3}. Ce que le Pape Iean a payé à Photius tresmeschant homme des salaires en lieu de supplices, a fait une grande tache à sa reputation, & de la chaire Pontificale. Delà, comme je pense, est arrivé (si toutesfois en un mensonge tres descouvert il y a peu avoir quelque apparence de verité) que Iean à cause de sa trop grande facilité d'esprit & mollesse, toute virilité mise bas entierement, rompu de courage, desnué de constance sacerdotale, & enervé de force, a esté dit par opprobre non Pape, comme Nicolas & Adrian, mais Papesse: Comme ainsi soit que celuy qui ne sçavoit resister à un Eunuque, & estoit vaincu par un demi homme, devoit estre plustost nommé femme qu'homme. Ainsi le nom de brocard est passé à l'esgard de la poste-
units.tr: It remains for us to try, if possible, to discover the door by which this story entered men's belief. The History of Erfurt, speaking of John VIII, successor of Adrian II, uses this language: Under the same King Charles the Fat, Pope John celebrated a Council at Erfurt, Hildebert (or rather Luitbert) being Archbishop of Mainz in the year 880. Note: this Pope was a woman, and would be the eighth if she were counted among the others. And Cardinal Baronius, aiming at the same object, adds his remark in these terms: What Pope John paid to Photius, a most wicked man, as wages instead of punishments, has left a great stain on his reputation and on the Papal chair. From this, as I think, it came about (if indeed in a very manifest lie there can be any appearance of truth) that John, because of his excessive softness of mind and his feebleness, having laid aside all manliness, broken in courage, stripped of priestly constancy and enfeebled in strength, was called in reproach not Pope, as Nicholas and Adrian were, but Papess: since he who could not resist a eunuch and was overcome by a half-man ought rather to be called a woman than a man. Thus the taunt passed, as regards posterity, from

units.la: {1} cap. 7. vrité ignorante des choses, en opinion de verité ; & cela a esté chanté par plusieurs, que Iean VIII Pape, a esté femme, & ainsi la fable espandue par le bruit commun a trouvé lieu en cette maniere. Qui de ceux qui ont conversé à Rome ignore, que souvent les Pontifes Romains sont en possession d'estre defchiquetez de brocads tout semblables, pour des causes plus legeres, par les mesdisans & oiseux ? Certes les choses que nous dirons cy dessous demonstreront que le Pontife Iean n'avoit pas provoqué contre soy les mesdisans seulement, mais aussi les sages & prudens.
units.tr: {1} chap. 7. ignorance of the facts into the opinion of truth; and it has been sung by many that Pope John VIII was a woman, and so the fable spread by common talk found its place in this way. Who among those who have lived in Rome does not know that the Roman Pontiffs are customarily torn to pieces with exactly similar taunts, for lighter causes, by slanderers and idlers? Indeed, the things we shall say below will show that Pontiff John had provoked against himself not only the slanderers but also the wise and prudent.

units.la: Or comme je ne dois pas entreprendre de faire bonne la caufe de ce Pape, qui en effet s'eft fort lafchement & imprudemment conduit ; j'advoüe que je ne puis acquiefcer abfolument à la conjecture du Card. Baronius, que je trouverois tres-vrayfemblable fi Rome plus que d'autres, avoit eu fujet de s'offencer des deportemens de Iean VIII I[?], ou fi elle avoit la premiere mis en avant le difcours de la Papesse. Mais voyant que le conte en eft nay premierement dans l'Allemagne, & que la nation Allemande a esté juftement indignée de ce que ( fans aucun efgard à la derniere volonté de l'Empereur Louys II, & au defir des peuples, & au droit que Louys Roy de Germanie avec ses enfans avoit de recueillir la succession de l'Empire & du Royaume de Lombardie) le Pape Iean VIII avoit en vraye femme, pris le parti de Charles le Chauve, qui ne luy fut en fin ni honorable, ni profitable ; j'enclinerois plustost à croire que l'aversion commune des Allemands contre sa memoire, & leur ressentiment contre sa mauvaise foy, auroient peu aider à produire le Roman de Marianus,esclos à Mayence, & delà espandu par tout.
units.tr: Now, since I am not to undertake to defend the cause of this Pope, who in fact conducted himself very cowardly and imprudently, I confess that I cannot fully agree with Cardinal Baronius's conjecture, which I would find very probable if Rome, more than others, had had cause to take offence at the conduct of John VIII, or if she had been the first to put forward the story of the Papess. But seeing that the tale was first born in Germany, and that the German nation was justly indignant that (without any regard to the last will of the Emperor Louis II, to the wishes of the peoples, and to the right which Louis, King of Germany, together with his children, had to inherit the Empire and the Kingdom of Lombardy) Pope John VIII had, womanishly, taken the side of Charles the Bald, which in the end proved neither honourable nor profitable to him; I would rather incline to believe that the common aversion of the Germans to his memory, and their resentment at his bad faith, may have helped to produce the romance of Marianus, hatched at Mainz and thence spread everywhere.

units.la: Aventin passe de Iean VIII, à Iean X posterieur de 30 ans, disant{1} Albert tresriche Prince de Toscane a eu Ravenne, Bologne, & Rome en sa puissance. Sa belle mere Theodora, garce noble & imperieuse, dominoit à Rome; & crea Evesque{2} Iean IX son amy, & l'establut[?] premierement sur les Boulonnois, puis sur les Ravennois, & enfin sur les Romains. D'où je croirois qu'est née la fable qui a temerairement divulgué qu'en ces temps là une femme ayt esté Evesque, & ayt esté appellée Iean. Mais Theodora ayant esté des le temps de Christophle en possession de tyrannizer Rome, & disposer du Papat, il y auroit eu plus
units.tr: Aventinus passes from John VIII to John X, some thirty years later, saying: Albert, a very rich prince of Tuscany, had Ravenna, Bologna and Rome in his power. His mother-in-law Theodora, a noble and imperious harlot, dominated Rome, and she made her friend John IX bishop, and set him first over Bologna, then over Ravenna, and finally over the Romans. From this, I would think, arose the fable that rashly spread the story that a woman was bishop in those times and was called John. But since Theodora had, from the time of Christopher, held the power to tyrannize Rome and dispose of the papacy, there would have been more reason to introduce a Papess Theodora than a Joan.

units.la: puis se remaria à Gui fils d'Albert Marquis de Tofcane, & de Berte fille du Roy Lothaire, & de Valdrade (dont elle ne laissa aucune lignée) & enfin espousa Hugues Roy d'Italie fils de Thibaut Comte d'Arles, & de Berte, par consequent frere uterin[?] de Guy. plus de raison d'introduire une Papesse Theodore, qu'une Ieanne.
units.tr: She then married Guy, son of Albert, Marquis of Tuscany, and of Berta, daughter of King Lothair, and of Valdrada (by whom she had no offspring). Finally she married Hugh, King of Italy, son of Theobald, Count of Arles, and of Berta, and so was a uterine brother of Guy.

units.la: Onufrius Panuinius apres une descente de 18 ans s'arrefte {1} à Iean XII fils d'Alberic Marquis non de Tofcane, comme il a pensé, mais de Campagne, fils de Marofie, & petit fils de Theodora, & dit, que ce Pape trainant apres foy une harde de garces, cherissoit entre toutes Ieanne, Rainiere, & Estienette; & que Ieanne (au gré de laquelle il se gouvernoit absolument) a esté depuis par quelque railleur appellée Papesse. Cependant tout ce discours (à le bien prendre) est sans fondement. car encore que Luitprand (sur l'autorité duquel on le veut appuyer) depeigne Iean XII comme un garnement, souillé de toutes sortes de vices; il ne dit rien de ce que l'on presuppose, & ne parle non plus de Ieanne que des atomes de Democrite; mais reproche seulement à Iean les amours de Rainiere, d'Estienette, d'une vefve nommée Anne, & de sa niepce, de laquelle il ne tesmoigne point qu'elle ayt esté plus en credit que les autres, ni qu'elle ayt porté le nom de Ieanne.
units.tr: Onuphrius Panvinius, after a descent of eighteen years, stops at John XII, son of Alberic, Marquis not of Tuscany, as he supposed, but of Campania, son of Marozia and grandson of Theodora. He says that this pope, dragging behind him a herd of harlots, cherished above all others Joan, Rainier and Stephanetta; and that Joan (at whose whim he governed absolutely) was later called the Papess by some mocker. Yet, rightly understood, all this account is without foundation. For although Liutprand (on whose authority they wish to rest it) depicts John XII as a scoundrel steeped in every kind of vice, he says nothing of what is presupposed, and speaks of Joan no more than of the atoms of Democritus. He reproaches John only with his love affairs with Rainier, Stephanetta, a widow named Anna, and his niece; he does not testify that any of these had more influence than the others, nor that she bore the name Joan.

units.la: Le Cardinal Bellarmin de son costé quitte l'Italie, & va chercher en Orient les traces de la pretendue Papesse. Le Pape Leon {2} (dit il) escrit que le bruit estoit constant, que plusieurs Eunuques ont esté assis au Patriarchat de Constantinople, & qu'une femme s'est glissée entre eux & a esté Patriarche. Peut estre que delà est née cette fable de Ieanne femme. Car le bruit estant que certaine femme avoit esté Pontife Constantinopolitain, & depuis (le nom de Constantinopolitain ayant esté peu à peu omis) le bruit & l'opinion d'une femme Pontife, & Pontife universel estans demeurez, quelques-uns en haine de l'Eglise Romaine ont commencé de dire que cette femme avoit esté Pontife Romain: & il est vray-semblable que ce bruit s'est levé environ le temps de Martinus Polonus.
units.tr: Cardinal Bellarmine, for his part, leaves Italy and goes looking in the East for traces of the supposed Papess. Pope Leo {2} (he says) writes that the rumour was constant, that several eunuchs have sat on the patriarchal throne of Constantinople, and that a woman slipped in among them and was patriarch. Perhaps from this arose the fable of a woman named Joan. For since there was a rumour that a certain woman had been Constantinopolitan Pontiff, and afterwards (the name Constantinopolitan having been gradually dropped) the rumour and opinion of a woman pontiff, and universal pontiff, remained, some, out of hatred of the Roman Church, began to say that this woman had been the Roman pontiff; and it is likely that this rumour arose around the time of Martin of Poland.

units.la: Notez derechef 1. Que Leon IX{1} ne dit pas proprement que le bruit estoit constant, mais qu'il estoit public, & ne faisoit pas de doute d'asseurer que cela estoit arrivé; 2. qu'il protefte quant à luy ne le vouloir pas croire; & 3. qu'ayant reproché l'an 1053 au Patriarche Michel la possibilité d'un tel evenement, Marianus (qui est mort 33 ans apres, & a donné quartier à sa Papesse entre Leon IV & Benoist III) ne permet pas que l'on recule la naissance du conte jusques au temps de Martinus Polonus.
units.tr: Note again: 1. that Leo IX does not properly say that the rumour was constant, but that it was public, and he did not doubt to assert that this had happened; 2. that he protests for his own part that he does not wish to believe it; and 3. that, having in 1053 reproached the Patriarch Michael with the possibility of such an event, Marianus (who died thirty-three years later, and gave a place to his Papess between Leo IV and Benedict III) does not allow us to push back the origin of the tale to the time of Martin of Poland.

units.la: En fin Leo Allatius {2} tourne teste vers l'Allemagne, & en tire cette remarque ;
units.tr: Finally, Leo Allatius turns his head towards Germany and draws from it this remark:

units.la: A Mayence en Germanie une femme nommée Thiota troubloit les affaires Ecclesiastiques ; comme les Annales des François & Sigebert en sa Chronique rapportent. Car elle s'appelloit nouvelle prophetesse, & usurpoit publiquement la charge d'enseigner & prescher. De la vint que plusieurs ayant laissé en arriere la doctrine sacrée, la suivirent comme maistresse addressée du Ciel. La chose estant descouverte puis apres, elle fut condamnée par jugement Synodal. Prenez Lecteur, ce que j'ay de certain & non douteus en l'esprit. Quelques hommes rudes & simples du siecle posterieur, oyans dire qu'entre Leon & Benoist, ou du moins en ce temps-là, certaine femme de Mayence avoit non seulement prophetizé, mais aussi presché, & fait toutes les autres functions par lesquelles les souverains Pontifes sont ornez ; & destournans leur esprit de cette femelle, qu'ils ne croyent pas mesme avoir pensé à un si grand crime, ils le tournent à la chaire principale, maistresse de tous, à sçavoir celle de Pierre, de laquelle ils sçavent fort bien que c'est là la charge, & la transferent de la Germanie en Italie, de Mayence à Rome : d'autres mefchans tirent malicieusement tout cela sur le tres-innocent throne de Pierre, & appliquent à la treshonorée Eglise Romaine une infamie Germanique. Pour pouvoir tromper plus aisement, ils veulent que cette Jeanne l'Angloise ayt efté de Mayence : & (les plaisans conteurs qu'ils sont) la vestent de tresbeaux recits , mais feints ; & l'exposent en veuë goffement parée : il ne me semble point (veu que le temps y respondent) que Iean de Mayence ait eu son origine d'ailleurs plus vray-semblablement , que de cette femme de Mayence. Toutesfois il est certain , qu'aucun de ceux qui ont parlé de Thiota , ne l'a faite originaire de Mayence , ni n'a dit qu'elle y ayt commencé ses jeux profanes , ni ne l'a produite au temps d'entre Leon & Benoist, ni n'a donné sujet à personne de croire qu'elle ayt esté condamnée ailleurs qu'à Mayence par l'Archevesque Rabanus & son Concile , ou que ce soit le propre office de l'Eglise Romaine de reprimer les attentats des faux prophetes : au contraire , ils revestent l'histoire de leur Thiota de tant de circonstances,que nul (à moins que d'avoir perdu le sens) ne sçauroit l'avoir transferée à la Jeanne de Marianus. Car apres avoir remarqué que Rabanus prit la place d'Otgier le Dimanche 27 Iuin 847, & qu'il tint par commandement du Roy Louys un Concile , environ le 1 Octobre ; ils adjoustent que Thiota (qui estoit en ce temps-là venue des parties d'Allemagne, c'est à dire du quartier de Suabe, & n'avoit pas peu troublé la paroisse de Salomon Evesque de Constance) y fut examinée en presence des Evesques assemblez dans le Monastere de S. Alban, convaincue d'avoir esté induite par un prestre à faire la prophetesse ; condamnée au fouët, & contrainte au silence: comment auroit il peu arriver à Marianus apres que les annales de Fulde, lieu celebre du diocese de Mayence, & celles de Mets, & Hernan qui escrivoit dans Richenaw monastere dependant de Constance, ont si expressement remarqué le temps, & le lieu, & l'effect de la condamnation de Thiota, fustigée l'an 847 en Octobre, six mois apres que Leon IV eust pris les resnes du gouvernement : comment dis-je luy feroit il arrivé de metamorphoser (dans Mayence mesme) cette Thiota en Jeanne ; la tirer d'Alemagne en Italie, & (nonobstant le descry & la punition deses faulses propheties) la mettre en possession du Papat ? Ce donc qu'Allatius a creu nous pouvoir debiter de bien certain & exempt de doute, demeure trescertainement douteux & mal asseuré.
units.tr: At Mainz in Germany a woman named Thiota was disturbing ecclesiastical affairs, as the Annals of the Franks and Sigebert in his Chronicle report. For she called herself a new prophetess, and publicly usurped the office of teaching and preaching. From this it came about that many, having left behind the sacred doctrine, followed her as a mistress sent from heaven. The matter being discovered afterwards, she was condemned by synodal judgment. Take note, reader, of what I hold as certain and beyond doubt in my mind. Some rude and simple men of a later age, hearing it said that between Leo and Benedict, or at least at that time, a certain woman of Mainz had not only prophesied but also preached, and performed all the other functions with which the sovereign pontiffs are adorned; and turning their minds away from this female, whom they do not believe ever even thought of so great a crime, they transfer it to the principal chair, mistress of all, namely that of Peter, of which they know very well that this is the office, and they carry it from Germany to Italy, from Mainz to Rome. Other wicked men maliciously pull all this onto the most innocent throne of Peter, and apply to the most honoured Roman Church a German infamy. To be able to deceive more easily, they want this Joan the Englishwoman to have been from Mainz: and (the entertaining storytellers that they are) they dress her in very beautiful accounts, but feigned; and they display her clumsily adorned: it does not seem to me (since the times answer for it) that John of Mainz had his origin elsewhere more plausibly than from this woman of Mainz. Nevertheless it is certain that none of those who have spoken of Thiota has made her a native of Mainz, nor said that she began there her profane antics, nor placed her at the time between Leo and Benedict, nor given anyone cause to believe that she was condemned anywhere other than at Mainz by Archbishop Rabanus and his council, or that it is the proper office of the Roman Church to repress the attempts of false prophets. On the contrary, they clothe the story of their Thiota with so many circumstances that no one (unless he had lost his wits) could have transferred it to the Joan of Marianus. For after remarking that Rabanus took the place of Otgar on Sunday 27 June 847, and that by command of King Louis he held a council around 1 October, they add that Thiota (who had at that time come from parts of Germany, that is, from the district of Swabia, and had not been able to trouble the parish of Bishop Salomon of Constance without consequence) was examined in the presence of the bishops assembled in the monastery of St. Alban, convicted of having been induced by a priest to play the prophetess, condemned to the whip, and compelled to silence. How could it have happened to Marianus, after the annals of Fulda, a famous place in the diocese of Mainz, and those of Metz, and Hermann, who wrote in the monastery of Reichenau, dependent on Constance, have so expressly noted the time, the place, and the effect of Thiota's condemnation, flogged in October 847, six months after Leo IV had taken the reins of government? How, I say, could it have happened to him to transform this Thiota (in Mainz itself) into Joan; to bring her out of Germany into Italy, and (despite the exposure and punishment of her false prophecies) to put her in possession of the papacy? What Allatius thought he could present to us as de quite certain and free from doubt, remains most certainly doubtful and insecure.

units.la: Apres luy je ne sçache personne qui ayt voulu exercer son esprit en des enquestes inutiles, pour un sujet qui n'en vaut pas la peine. Car en conscience, que nous en revieneviendroit il, quand nous aurions descouvert le blanc sur lequel Marianus a visé, & de quel fonds sa bourde a tiré l'occasion de s'espandre? Où en ferions nous, s'il nous falloit deviner sur quoy se font fondez les auteurs de tant de Romans, qui trouvent jusques à present du credit dans l'opinion du commun? D'où, par exemple, nous sont venus les contes, de la cheute du temple de la paix à Rome le jour propre de la naissance du fils de Dieu, resuscité & monté dans les Cieux 42 ans devant que Vespasian l'eust basti? de l'equippée de Cyriacus quittant le Papat pour se mettre à la teste des onze mille vierges; du long sommeil des sept dormans; du pretendu Christianisme de l'Empereur Philippe successeur & meurtrier du jeune Gordian : de la conversion miraculeuse de Iudas inventeur de la vraye Croix, & depuis Evesque de Ierusalem sous le nom de Cyriacus; de la guerison de l'Empereur Constantin, & de son Baptesme par S. Silvestre; de la sortie de Trajan hors des enfers accordée aux prieres de S. Gregoire; & (pour dire un mot en passant des fables concernans nostre France) du siege de Paris sous le regne de Louys le Debonnaire par le Geant Isaure, dont on monstre la sepulture au monastere de S. Germain, & du supplice d'Herbert II du nom Comte de Vermandois, pendu (si ceux de Laon en sont creus) pres de leur ville sur le mont appellé jusques aujourd'huy le mont Hebert ? Qui a peu mouvoir divers auteurs Latins à placer apres Liberius, un Leon diffamé par eux à cause de son Arianisme, & de la persecution de nostre S. Hilaire : ou à inventer un Fabian intrus (à leur dire) entre Vigilius & Pelagius ; & un Paul avec un Estienne interposez par eux mesmes entre Benoist III & Nicolas premier ? Qu'il nous suffise que tous ces contes, sont contes & rien plus : que quand tout le monde les tiendroit pour oracles, il ne seroit pas en son pouvoir de leur faire changer de nature, & à l'opposite, que quand la verité (opprimée par la tyrannie des prejugez, & bravée par la vanité des Romans, & trahie par l'oubly, ou par la lascheté des hommes) auroit à se voir pour quelque temps mesconnue & desdaignée; ni sa solitude ne pourroit luy tourner à honte, ni l'effort de ses ennemis la faire decheoir de sa dignité, ni la belle apparence des fables causer de l'eclipse à sa divine lumiere : puis qu'elle est fille du Dieu de gloire, qui la fera finalement riompher avec gloire de tous fes ennemis, ans que ni la malice des temps, ni les difgraces aufquelles l'infirmité humaine a ccouftumé de fe rendre, foient capables de la forcer à fe renier foy mefme: elle levera à la fin (comme du fein des fouffres) fa tefte victorieufe, & (felon que difoit le Poete) ayant esté fubmergée au plus profond des flots, elle en fortira plus belle, & fera l'admiration & la joye de ceux qui l'auront ignorée.
units.tr: After him I know of no one who has been willing to exercise his wits on pointless inquiries into a subject not worth the trouble. For in all conscience, what would we gain if we had discovered the target at which Marianus aimed, and the source from which his fable drew its occasion to spread? Where would we be if we had to guess what foundations lay under the many romances that still find credit in the common opinion? Whence, for example, came the tales of the fall of the Temple of Peace at Rome on the very day of the Son of God's birth, the Son who had risen and ascended into heaven forty-two years before Vespasian built it; of Cyriacus leaving the papacy to put himself at the head of the eleven thousand virgins; of the long sleep of the seven sleepers; of the pretended Christianity of the Emperor Philip, successor and murderer of the young Gordian; of the miraculous conversion of Judas, discoverer of the true Cross and afterwards bishop of Jerusalem under the name of Cyriacus; of the healing of the Emperor Constantine and his baptism by St Silvester; of the release of Trajan from hell granted to the prayers of St Gregory; and (to say a word in passing about the fables concerning our own France) of the siege of Paris under the reign of Louis the Debonair by the giant Isaure, whose tomb is shown in the monastery of St Germain, and of the execution of Herbert II, count of Vermandois, who was hanged (if the people of Laon are to be believed) near their town, on the hill still called to this day Mont Hebert? What moved various Latin writers to place after Liberius a Leo, defamed by them because of his Arianism and his persecution of our St Hilary; or to invent a Fabian, an intruder (as they say), between Vigilius and Pelagius; and a Paul and a Stephen, which they themselves inserted between Benedict III and Nicholas I? Let it suffice us that all these stories are stories and nothing more: that even if the whole world held them for oracles, it would not be in its power to change their nature. And conversely, when the truth (oppressed by the tyranny of prejudice, defied by the vanity of romances, and betrayed by forgetfulness or by the cowardice of men) finds itself for a time unrecognised and disdained, its solitude cannot turn to its shame, nor can the efforts of its enemies cause it to fall from its dignity, nor can the fair appearance of fables bring an eclipse upon its divine light. For it is the daughter of the God of glory, who will at last cause it to triumph gloriously over all its enemies, so that neither the malice of the times nor the misfortunes to which human weakness is accustomed to yield can force it to deny itself. In the end it will raise its victorious head (as from the bosom of the clouds) and, as the poet said, having been submerged in the depths of the waves, it will emerge more beautiful, and will be the admiration and joy of those who had been ignorant of it.

units.la: Veu donc qu'elle fe trouve fi evidente du cofté des auteurs, qui ont efcrit entre les années 850 & 1050 de noftre Seigneur, que toutes leurs depofitions s'accordans compofent un corps bien ajufté, & propofent les evenemens dont on difpute, avec une aufli grande clarté que s'ils en avoient tiré le crayon avec un ray du Soleil, & que les efcrivains posterieurs font pleins de contradictions & incompatibilitez, tant avec les antecedens qu'avec eux mefmes: il femble que leur opinion (de quelque longueur de cours qu'elle fe puiffe vanter) ne merite point de meilleur traittement, que d'eftre (par la commune voix de tous ceux qui fe rendent dociles à la raifon) condamnée au billon.
units.tr: Since, then, the truth is so evident on the side of the authors who wrote between the years 850 and 1050 of our Lord, that all their testimonies, agreeing together, form a well-fitted body and set out the events in dispute with as much clarity as if they had traced them with a ray of the sun; and since the later writers are full of contradictions and incompatibilities, both with the earlier ones and with themselves; it seems that their opinion (however long a run it may boast of) deserves no better treatment than to be condemned, by the common voice of all who yield to reason, as base coin.

units.la: Mais pour la garantir de ce prejudice, & empescher de le causer, les homme[?] (selon que leurs inclinations sont disposées) allèguent diverses exceptions. Les[?] uns soustiennent que la supposition de la[?] Papesse estant du rang des choses totalement indifferentes, & concernant un fait d'histoire de fort petite consequence, il[?] ne seroit pas raisonnable de les engager à se determiner si precisement, que non seulement ils eussent à prendre necessairement parti, mais aussi à desadvoüer ceux qui en pourroient faire refus. Et je supplie ceux-la de considerer, qu'ils posent (sans y penser) un fondement tresfaux.
units.tr: But to protect it from this harm, and to keep anyone from inflicting it, men (according as their inclinations are disposed) put forward various objections. Some maintain that since the supposed Papess belongs to the class of things wholly indifferent, and concerns a matter of history of very little consequence, it would not be reasonable to bind them to decide so precisely that they would have to take a side necessarily, and also to disown those who might refuse to do so. And I beg those people to consider that they lay, without thinking, a very false foundation.

units.la: Car encore que la fiction de la Papesse, soit (en effet) de fort petite, ou mesme de nulle consequence, pour les controverses d'à present : les gens de bien ne la peuvent nullement passer pour une chose indifferente ; le titre qu'ils portent de Chrestiens, & de zelateurs de la verité, les obligeant expressement à renoncer à tout ce qui la choque, soit directement soit indirectement : & par consequent à se declarer ennemis formels des fables; empescher (autant que leur pouvoir le permettra) les longues consequences que quelques uns s'efforcent d'en tirer ; eloigner avec le mesme soin les applications de l'Escriture, que l'on pourroit s'imaginer, pour leur acquerir de la probabilité, ou du poids; & sur tout se tenir religieusement à la protestation de S. Paul ; {1}nous ne pouvons rien conre la verité, mais pour la verité. Joint que leur accordant de grace l'indifference qu'ils presupposent, & prenant droit de la concession d'icelle) on en pourroit conclurre (directement contre leur intention) qu'ils seroient tenus de donner, au moins, une aussi facile audience aux impugnateurs de l'opinion de Marianus, qu'à ceux qui la defendent; se souvenans que cela mesme que la verité & la raison parlent pour les premiers, meriteroit bien de chacun une particuliere faveur.
units.tr: For although the fiction of the Papess is in fact of very little, or even no, consequence for the controversies of the present day, good people cannot in any way regard it as a matter of indifference. The title they bear of Christians and of zealots for the truth expressly obliges them to renounce everything that offends it, whether directly or indirectly; and consequently to declare themselves formal enemies of the fables; to prevent, as far as their power allows, the far-reaching consequences that some strive to draw from them; to keep away with the same care the applications of Scripture that one might imagine in order to win them probability or weight; and above all to hold religiously to the protest of St Paul: {1} we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth. Moreover, if we grant them the indifference they presuppose, and take advantage of that concession, one could conclude (directly against their intention) that they would be bound to give at least as ready a hearing to the opponents of Marianus's opinion as to those who defend it; remembering that the very fact that truth and reason speak for the former ought to earn each of them a particular favour.

units.la: D'autres disent, que ce seroit une chose fort dure, de requerir d'eux qu'ils entreprissent de nager contre le torrent d'une opinion qui a si long temps prevalu ; veu mesme qu'elle a esté, & est encore, defendue par leurs amis ; & qu'eux mesmes l'ont suivie Et à la verité j'advoüe, que c'est un exercice mal plaisant, de s'employer à relever les defauts, où l'infirmité, l'incurie, & l'oubly, peuvent avoir jetté les esprits des hommes ; que ces defauts font (en qui que ce soit) des choses honteuses d'elles mesmes, & que nul ne peut les trouver en fon ame , ni en fes amis, fans rougir , c pour foy , ou pour eux. Mais je fouftiet auffi que s'il y a de la honte à faillir, il n en peut avoir à fe corriger, & que le Chr ftien s'en feroit une tres-grande,fi(mefcor noiffant fa propre fragilité ) il dedaigno l'imitation de l'ingenuité de ce pauvi Payen qui crioit, {1} je fuis homme, je ne penj pas avoir exemption d'aucune des chofes humaines; & fi par un fi injufte defdain il s'en gageoit à debattre à l'encontre du fenti ment de fa propre confcience , & de la ve rité. En effet, comme dire que nous n pouvons nous departir d'une opinion , pource qu'elle eft ou a efté commune , fe roit oppofer tres-mal à propos la multitu de à la vérité , fans penfer à la confequenc de cette defence divine, {2} Tu n'enfuivra point la multitude , pour maifaire ; & fan vouloir prefter l'oreille à ces fages adver tiffemens de Theodoret , {3} Ce'luy qui man que de preuves , & pourtant recourt à la mul titude , confesse qu'il succombe. Tu me porte dans la veuë la multitude , comme menaçan Dieu du baftiment d'une feconde tour. Si tu fortifies le menfonge par la multitude , tu mon ftres le rengrement du grief: car plus il y a de gens engagez au mal , & plus la calamité eft grande. Et d'ailleurs comme advouer que nous ne pouvons desdire nos amis en leurs fautes, seroit 1.[?] intenter une accusation tacite contre l'iniquité de nos jugemens partiaux, qui prefereroient l'interest des hommes à celuy de la verité ; & 2 publier (au prejudice de noftre reputation) que nos arrests seroient dictez par la faveur, sans connoissance de cause, & sans raison, contre le sentiment de laquelle prendre des resolutions, seroit esteindre (par un effort contraire à noftre bien) la lumiere que la bonté de Dieu a daigné allumer en nos ames, & (nous opposant en quelque forte à sa sagesse) descouvrir que nous avons moins profité en l'escole de l'Eglise, que les Philosophes & Poetes en celle de la nature, l'un disant: {1}Platon est mon amy & la verité encore plus ; L'autre se glorifiant d'estre tellement des-interesse, qu'il {2}n'estoit obligé par serment à tenir la parole d' aucun maistre.Et le fils de Dieu nous ayant prescrit noftre devoir par ce notable enseignement : {3}Ne soyez point appellez noftre Maistre, car un seul est vostre Docteur, à sçavoir Christ.Ioint que S. Iacques {4}nous a dit en suitte : Ne soyez point plusieurs Maistres:& S. Paul, {5}Ne soyez point serfs des hommes ; item {6}Esprouvez toutes choses, retenez ce qui est bon. Et S. Augustin de par eux
units.tr: Others will say that it would be very harsh to ask them to undertake to swim against the stream of an opinion that has prevailed for so long, especially since it has been, and still is, defended by their friends, and since they themselves have followed it. Indeed I confess that it is an unpleasant exercise to set about exposing the faults into which weakness, carelessness and forgetfulness may have cast men's minds. Such faults are shameful in themselves in whomever they are found, and no one can discover them in his own soul or in his friends without blushing, either for himself or for them. But I maintain also that if there is shame in erring, there can be none in correcting oneself, and that a Christian would bring great shame upon himself if, knowing his own frailty, he disdained to imitate the candour of that humble pagan who cried, I am a man; I do not think I am exempt from any of the things that belong to men, and if through such an unjust disdain he bound himself to dispute against the feeling of his own conscience and against the truth. For, just as to say that we cannot depart from an opinion because it is, or has been, common would be to set the multitude very wrongly against the truth, forgetting the consequence of that divine prohibition, You shall not follow the multitude to do evil, and refusing to listen to the wise warnings of Theodoret: He who lacks proofs and yet has recourse to the multitude confesses that he is defeated. You set the multitude before your eyes, as if threatening God with the building of a second tower. If you strengthen a falsehood by the multitude, you show the enlargement of the wrong, for the more people are engaged in evil, the greater the calamity. Moreover, to admit that we cannot unsay our friends' faults would be, first, to bring a tacit accusation against the iniquity of our partial judgments, which prefer the interest of men to that of the truth; and second, to proclaim (to the detriment of our reputation) that our decisions are dictated by favour, without knowledge of the case and without reason. To take resolutions against the judgment of reason would be to extinguish, by an effort contrary to our own good, the light that the goodness of God has deigned to kindle in our souls, and (opposing ourselves in some measure to his wisdom) to discover that we have profited less in the school of the Church than the philosophers and poets have in the school of nature. One of them said: Plato is my friend, but the truth is still more my friend; the other, glorying in being so disinterested, said that he was not bound by oath to swear by the words of any master. And the Son of God, having prescribed our duty by this notable teaching: Do not be called Master, for one is your Teacher, namely Christ. Add to this that St James told us next: Do not be many masters; and St Paul: Do not become slaves of men; likewise: Test all things, hold fast to what is good. And St Augustine, on their behalf:

units.la: {6} 1 Thes. 5.21. tous: {1}C'est le plus seur, que nous qui parlons, & vous qui oyez, nous reconnoissions condisciples sous un seul maistre ; en effet c'est le plus seur, & il est expedient, que vous nous oyez, non comme Maistres, mais comme condisciples.
units.tr: {6} 1 Thess. 5.21. All: It is safest that we who speak and you who hear acknowledge one another as fellow disciples under one Master; indeed it is safest, and it is expedient, that you hear us not as masters but as fellow disciples.

units.la: Aussi mettre en avant qu'il nous est impossible de desmordre des opinions que nous avons une fois defendues, & encore plus de les desadvoüer hautement, feroit monstrer 1 que nous nous aimerions beaucoup plus, que la verité, 2 que nous ferions hommes à rendre par nostre affectation toutes sortes de mesprises irremediables, 3 que nous aurions laschement abandonné nos ames à la tyrannie de nostre opiniastreté, & fort mal digeré l'ordonnance que le grand Maistre nous a faite en son Euangile, de renoncer à nous mesmes pour estre vrayement ses discip'es ; de ne point chercher nostre propre ; d'aimer la verité (de quelque genre & importance qu'elle soit) à cause d'elle mesme, & de la gloire de son auteur ; & de ne faire aucun estat ni de nous, ni de nos amis, ni de tout le monde ensemble, à comparaison de son interest.
units.tr: To put forward that it is impossible for us to abandon opinions we have once defended, and still more to disavow them openly, would be to show, first, that we love ourselves far more than the truth; second, that we would be men who, through our self-regard, cause all kinds of irremediable mistakes; third, that we would have cowardly surrendered our souls to the tyranny of our own obstinacy, and would have badly digested the command that the great Master gave us in his Gospel: to deny ourselves in order to be truly his disciples, not to seek our own, to love the truth (of whatever kind and importance it may be) for its own sake and for the glory of its author, and to set no value on ourselves, on our friends, or on the whole world together in comparison with his interest.

units.la: D'autres en fin pourront dire, que rien ne les oblige à guerir les playes que Rome a bien voulu fe faire de fes mains propres ; que c'eft à elle à y remedier comme elle pourra ; & que ceux qui font en poffession d'en tirer avantage à son prejudice, ne s'en doivent pas departir. Ces pensées sont fort plausibles ; mais plus je les confidere, & moins je les trouve de mife. Car devons nous aimer la verité comme mercenaires, à caufe seulement qu'elle nous est utile, & non plustoft comme enfans bien instruits, à caufe qu'elle est nostre mere & souverainement aimable ? entreprendrons nous de luy faire perdre quelque chose de son prix, des l'heure que nous luy aurons ouy dire un mot contre quelqu'unde nos prejugez, & pour l'efclaircissement de quelque fait concernant l'interest de ceux qui ne veulent pas estre bien avec nous ? ou ferons nous en liberté de quitter son interest, là où nous nous ferons apperceus qu'il ne peut compatir en tout avec le nostre ?
units.tr: Others may finally say that nothing obliges them to heal the wounds that Rome has been pleased to inflict with her own hands; that it is for her to remedy them as she can; and that those who are in possession of profiting from them to her detriment ought not to give them up. These thoughts are very plausible, but the more I consider them, the less I find them appropriate. For ought we to love the truth as hired labourers, only because it is useful to us, and not rather as well-taught children, because it is our mother and supremely lovable? Shall we undertake to make it lose something of its worth, as soon as we have heard it say a word against one of our prejudices, or in clarifying some matter that touches the interest of those who do not wish to be on good terms with us? Or shall we be free to abandon its interest at the point where we perceive that it cannot agree in every respect with our own?

units.la: En cas que l'adjonction d'un mensonge avoüé durant quelque temps, par ceux là mesme qui en font grevez, & que l'on presuppose d'ailleurs avoir tort, puisse leur tourner en accroissement de prejudice, faudra t'il faire fondement certain de leur erreur reconnu, chercher contre eux le gain legitime de la bonne cause dans l'employ d'une fausseté de si belle apparence, qu'elle ayt peu leur causer à eux mesmes de l'esblouïssement ? ou bien devra t'on souffrir que ceux qui font profession formelle de combattre pour la vraye pieté contre les fables, donnent à la pieté les fables des autres, pour seconds & pour instrumens de vengeance : comme s'il estoit permis à aucun de s'armer honteusement des artifices du mensonge, {1}faire mal afin que bien en advienne, & s'imaginer que la verité de Dieu doive jamais par la menterie (soit conceuë,soit maintenue chez qui que l'on puisse penser) estre plus abondante à sa gloire ? Comme nul ne doit estre porté à la confession & défense d'aucune verité, par la seule complaisance dont on pourroit flatter la passion de ceux qui s'en promettent quelque soulagement : mais par le desir seul de donner gloire à Dieu en l'hommage franc & sincere d'une bonne conscience : Aucun n'a le droit de nier, ou dissimuler la verité, par despit de ce qu'elle autorize le readvis de ceux qui (s'estans eux mesmes trompez en la suppo-sition de quelque disgrace imaginaire) auroient persuadé à d'autres qu'ils y estoient tombez en effet. Si ceux qui se font ont mefcontez à leur dommage ont à fe laindre de leur inadvertence precedente, e n'eft pas à d'autres à leur donner occasion de faire plainte contre leur exceffive lureté , afin que je ne die contre leur mauaife foy;& fi l'on peut bien(fans faire tort ceux qui fe font mefpris) conclurre de la confeffion qu'ils ont faite à leur prejudice, qu'ils avoient fort mauvaife opinion d'eux nesmes ; apres qu'il eft apparu que la perfuafion fondée fur cette fausse confeffion eftoit vaine , elle ne fe peut plus maintenir par aucun,qu'avec lefion de la verité & fincerité. Car il y auroit peu de grace & d'ingenuité à faire trophée d'une beveuë,dont celuy qui l'avoit faite fe feroit en fin delivré; & (au lieu de confiderer fagement que {1}le confentement de celuy qui erre eft nul) fermer les yeux à toutes autres confiderations que de ce tel quel confentement, voire fe les crever, pluftoft que de permettre à la lumiere de la verité d'y faire fon entrée , pour bannir par fa prefence les prejugez inveterez & les imaginations creufes.
units.tr: Suppose that the addition of a lie, admitted for some time by those very people who are burdened by it, and presupposed to be in the wrong otherwise, could turn to their increased harm. Shall we then make it a firm foundation to take their recognised error, and seek against them the legitimate gain of the good cause by the use of a falsehood so fair in appearance that it may have dazzled even them? Or must we suffer those who make formal profession of fighting for true piety against fables to give the fables of others as allies and instruments of vengeance for piety? As if anyone were permitted to arm himself shamefully with the artifices of lies, to do evil so that good may come of it, and to imagine that the truth of God should ever, through a lie (whether conceived or maintained by whomever one may think), abound more to his glory? Just as no one ought to be moved to confess and defend any truth merely by the complaisance with which one might flatter the passion of those who promise themselves some relief from it, but only by the sole desire to give glory to God in the frank and sincere homage of a good conscience: no one has the right to deny or dissemble the truth out of spite that it authorises the retraction of those who, having themselves been deceived in supposing some imaginary disgrace, had persuaded others that they had in fact fallen into it. If those who have been mistaken to their own loss have cause to complain of their earlier inadvertence, it is not for others to give them occasion to complain of their excessive harshness, not to say of their bad faith. And if one may well conclude (without wronging those who have been mistaken) from the confession they made to their own prejudice that they had a very poor opinion of themselves, then, once it has appeared that the persuasion founded on that false confession was vain, it can no longer be maintained by anyone except with injury to truth and sincerity. For there would be little grace and candour in making a trophy of an error from which the one who made it has at last freed himself; and (instead of wisely considering that the consent of one who errs is void) in closing one's eyes to every consideration other than that mere consent, indeed in putting them out, rather than allowing the light of truth to enter there to banish by its presence long-rooted prejudices and empty imaginings.

units.la: Ces procedures pourroient bien avoir lieu au regne de la vengeance & du despit, tyrans aveugles & eftourdis , d'ont l'empires'eftablit felon les vifées {2}de la sapience du monde qui est folie devant Dieu; mais elle[?] ne feront jamais recevables au regne de l[?] charité fondé dans le cœur des saints pa[?] l'Euangile de grace, qui est {1}la puissance a Dieu en sa!ut a tout croyant. Car tout le fruit qu'elles sçauroient produire, sera d'effarou[?]cher de plus en plus les esprits, & (au lieu d'induire ceux qui sont en debat pour la religion, à donner gloire à Dieu par la conversion de leurs ames à sa paix, & tendre à l'edification du prochain, par l'adveu ingenu de ce qui peut estre relasché sans dommage de la verité, & sans violement de l'integrité de la foy, ) les porter à une impetuosité egalement obstinée & violente; pour s'entretenir en des querelles de pointilles, & donner des batailles de mots, & accroistre la haine & l'irritation, que tous sçavent & experimentent n'avoir eu que trop de credit jusqu'icy.
units.tr: These proceedings might well have a place in the reign of vengeance and spite, those blind and reckless tyrants whose empire is established according to the aims of {2}the wisdom of this world, which is foolishness before God. But they can never be admissible in the reign of charity, founded in the hearts of the saints by the Gospel of grace, which is {1}the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth. For all the fruit they could possibly produce will be to frighten minds more and more, and (instead of leading those who are in dispute over religion to give glory to God by converting their souls to his peace, and to strive for the edification of their neighbour, by frankly acknowledging what may be relaxed without harm to the truth and without violating the integrity of the faith) to drive them into an impetuosity that is equally obstinate and violent, so that they keep up quarrels over trifles, wage battles of words, and increase the hatred and irritation which everyone knows and has experienced all too well until now.

units.la: Que donc les bonnes ames & candides n'ayent point de regret, d'abandonner la defense d'un Roman, debité cy devant de la part de Rome mesme pour histoire; puis qu'en effet ce n'est autre chose qu'un Roman: qu'elles ne craignent point qu'il y ayt à perdre pour elles en la perte d'une fable, & de la consequence qu'elle sembloit tirer apres soy de quelque avanige imaginaire. C'eft assez que la verité trouve le fien tout entier, & un gain afsuré; & qu'en luy donnant genereusement le prix de sa victoire, ceux qui l'embrafent d'affection, monstrent à l'univers l'exemple d'une ingenuité vrayment Chretienne, qui ne trouve ni juste ni honorable d'attendre que les convictions viennent d'ailleurs[?], pour les forcer de se rendre à la raifon; mais immolent de bon cœur, comme un sacrifice vrayement {1}raifonnable & plaisant à Dieu, tous leurs interests & tous les avantages que les erreurs defendus de longue main par d'autres, pourroient leur promettre, à la gloire seule de la pieté, & de la verité.
units.tr: Let the good and sincere souls therefore have no regret in abandoning the defence of a romance, once put forward by Rome itself as history; since in truth it is nothing but a romance. Let them not fear that they lose anything in losing a fable, or in losing the advantage which it seemed to bring with it, some imaginary benefit. It is enough that the truth recovers all that is its own, and a sure gain; and that, by generously giving it the prize of its victory, those who embrace it with affection show the world an example of truly Christian candour, which finds it neither right nor honourable to wait until convictions come from elsewhere to force them to yield to reason, but which sacrifices from the heart, as a truly {1}reasonable and acceptable to God sacrifice, all their interests and all the advantages that the errors long defended by others might promise them, for the sole glory of piety and of truth.

units.la: Qu'ils se souviennent que si autresfois la loy prononçoit {2}malediction, contre celuy qui fait fourvoyer l'aveugle en chemin ; & ordonnoit à l'ennemy de {3}ramener à son ennemy son bœuf ou son asne esgarez ; la religion Chrestienne requiert encor quelque chose de plus de ses professeurs : il faut oster les pierres d'achoppement du chemin de ceux que l'on croid manquer de lumiere, porter la lumiere de la verité sur tout, & tendre la main de la charité par tout. Que les plus scrupuleux pensent, que s'ils consentent & contribuent au descri desiré, & poursuivi ardamment par Rome, de cette fausse piece dont elle mesme avoit autrefois approuvé, voire entrepris le debit ; ils ne sont pas induits à s'y porter pour la gratifier, mais seulement pour venger l'injure de la verité, blessée par l'introduction des happelourdes dans le commerce spirituel des Chrestiens: & sans mettre en aucune consideration si Rome recevra, ou ne recevra pas de la satisfaction d'un si franc procedé.
units.tr: Let them remember that if formerly the law pronounced {2}a curse upon him who causeth the blind to wander out of the way, and ordered the enemy to {3}bring back to his enemy his ox or his ass gone astray, the Christian religion requires still more of its professors. They must remove the stumbling blocks from the path of those whom one believes to lack light, bring the light of truth to bear on everything, and extend the hand of charity everywhere. Let the most scrupulous consider that if they consent to and help the desired and ardently pursued proclamation by Rome of this false piece, which Rome itself had formerly approved and even undertaken to put about, they are not induced to act thus to please her, but only to avenge the wrong done to the truth, wounded by the introduction of impostures into the spiritual commerce of Christians; and without taking into any consideration whether Rome will or will not be satisfied by so frank a procedure.

units.la: Et si l'on veut (à toute force) qu'ils s'affermissent dans le dessein de remporter, outre l'avantage direct de la verité, quelque utilité particuliere de la preconization que les Docteurs de l'Eglise Romaine ont faite 400 ans durant de leur Papesse ; qu'ils considerent que tout le gain reel qu'ils en ont jamais peu tirer, leur demeure & demeurera à tousjours ; à sçavoir que Rome a esté en si estrange estime entre ses enfans, voire entre ses propres Papes, que rien de ce qui se pourroit penser & dire avec atteinte à sa reputation, pour estrange & honteux qu'il fust, n'a semblé ni incroyable, ni eloigné de la vray-semblance, ni douteux ; mais a esté creu & publié, & maintenu constamment durant plusieurs siecles. Ioint que (depuis qu'elle revenue à foy mesme) elle s'est fait enre deux torts irreparables, & qui luy ent aujourd'huy le moyen de perfuar qu'en niant la fable de la Papesse, fes avocats ayent procedé de bonne foy, & vi leur propre sentiment. Le premier, rs qu'elle a demoli la rue, où les anciens etendoient que le scandaleux accoucheent de leur Jean l'Anglois estoit arrivé. Car ecore que l'on die que le Pape Sixte V, fait abbattre pour l'eflargir, & dresser cordeau: ceux d'entre les estrangers & Romains[?] naturels qui considereront que procession continue à passer par une autre rue qui n'est pas plus large, & qui allonge son chemin, ne pourront se figur qu'elle prene ce destour, qu'en souvenance de l'infame accident de la pretendue Jeanne.
units.tr: And if one insists (at all costs) that they should be resolved to gain, beyond the direct advantage of the truth, some particular usefulness from the proclamation which the teachers of the Roman Church have made for 400 years concerning their Papess, let them consider that all the real gain they have ever been able to draw from it remains and will always remain with them: namely, that Rome has been held in such strange esteem among her children, and even among her own Popes, that nothing which could be thought or said to the injury of her reputation, however strange and shameful it might be, has seemed incredible, remote from probability, or doubtful; but has been believed, published and steadfastly maintained for several centuries. Moreover, since she came back to herself, she has committed two irreparable wrongs, which today give her the means to persuade people that in denying the fable of the Papess her advocates have acted in good faith and according to their own opinion. The first is that she has demolished the street where the old writers said that the scandalous childbirth of their John the Englishman had taken place. For although it is said that Pope Sixtus V had it knocked down in order to widen it and make it straight as a line, those foreigners and native Romans who consider that the procession continues to pass through another street which is no wider, and which lengthens its route, cannot imagine that it takes this detour except in remembrance of the infamous incident of the so-called Joan.

units.la: Le second,lors qu'elle a osté de sa niche fait disparoir au temps, soit de Pie V, soit de Sixte V, soit de Clement VIII, veu que l'on n'en est pas d'accord) la statue que l'on s'imaginoit representer cette [?]arce imaginaire. Car si c'estoit en effet la figure d'une nouvelle accouchée, (comme Thierry de Niem,. & plusieurs autres aprés luy ont presupposé) pourquoy entrerenant de s'inscrire en faux contre le sembloit attesté par ce monu[illegible, ~4 letters] public, n'a t'on (sans l'arracher de son taché d'en monstrer l'origine, & le vra[?] usage, ou mesme l'abus? Et si c'estoit (cor[illegible, ~3 letters] soustient le Cardinal Bellarmin) {1} le fim[?] cre d'un sacrificateur payen, pourquoy l'a[?] lissant a t'on privé les curieux du moyen[?] de tirer, de l'inspection qu'ils en eussent faire à tous momens, l'esclaircissemen[t?] l'erreur de Thierry de Niem, le premie[r?] de tous ceux qui en ont parlé? Il est dor[?] craindre que le fracas & l'eloignement [?] tier, de cette piece celebre dans l'opini[on?] des hommes qui ont vescu depuis 250 a[?] ne face long temps l'effet dont un Cardi[nal?] tresjudicieux menaçoit le Pape Sixte V,c[?] vouloit il y a tantoft 58 ans, faire jetter Pasquin & le Marforio dans le Tibre, disa[?] que s'ils y estoient precipitez, ils deviendroient grenoüilles & crieroient delà avec une voix plus haute & plusforte que jamais. Car quiconqu[e?] sçaura le soin que l'on a pris d'abolir un marque publique, prise par le commu[n?] pour un monument particulier de la Pa[?] pesse Ieanne, fera facilement entreten[u?] dans la creance qu'elle avoit esté premierement erigée à son occasion.
units.tr: The second is that she removed from its niche and made disappear, at the time (for people do not agree whether it was Pius V, Sixtus V or Clement VIII) the statue that was imagined to represent that imaginary woman. For if it was in fact the figure of a newly delivered mother (as Dietrich of Niem and several others after him have presupposed), why, instead of trying to contradict what seemed attested by that public monument, did they not (without tearing it from its place) show its origin and its true use, or even its abuse? And if it was (as Cardinal Bellarmine maintains) {1}the image of a pagan priest, why by suppressing it have they deprived the curious of the means of drawing from its inspection, which they could make at every moment, the clearing up of the error of Dietrich of Niem, the first of all those who have spoken of it? It is certainly to be feared that the noise and the removal of this piece, so celebrated in the opinion of men who have lived since, will for a long time produce the effect with which a very judicious Cardinal threatened Pope Sixtus V, about 58 years ago, when he wished to have Pasquin and Marforio thrown into the Tiber, saying that if they were cast in, they would become frogs and would croak from there with a voice higher and stronger than ever. For whoever knows the care that has been taken to abolish a public mark, taken by the common people for a particular monument of the Papess Joan, will easily be kept in the belief that it was first erected on her account.

units.la: Il faut que ceux qui sont studieux, conssans[?] qu'il y va du danger de leur ame, que rien ne doit estre premier en consideration que la verité ; & pensans de plus les maux que la haine & preoccupation engendrent, se rendent auditeurs communs à ceux qui parlent des deux costez ; non toutesfois egaux, &c.
units.tr: Those who are studious must bear in mind that their soul's salvation is at stake, that nothing should take precedence in their consideration except the truth. Thinking also of the evils that hatred and prejudice produce, they should make themselves willing hearers of those who speak on both sides, though not equally so, etc.
